Thank your for your comments. 

> W1: Generalisability: The study's generalisability is a concern, as the analysis is limited to a single model architecture (OLMo 2, 1B) and primarily the target domain of Mathematics.

> Q1: Could the authors provide supplementary results from more/larger models and more target domains to strengthen the support for the generalisability of the observed phenomena?

We have carried out the experiments on additional domains: instruction data and code, as well as on 7B parameters models. It has allowed us to confirm the findings regarding domain connectivity, and to uncover attention head heterogeneity with regard to CPT behavior. For details, and for our reasoning for choosing OLMo backbone please refer to the general comment above, and to the updated sections 4.4 and 4.5 in main text.

> W2: Lack of Theoretical Depth: While the experiments are comprehensive, the theoretical explanations for the observed phenomena, such as the complex spectral structures and the improved interpolation quality, remain preliminary. The work would benefit from more rigorous mathematical modeling and analysis.
 
> Q2: Regarding the geometric interpretation of the "domain connectivity" interpolation path: The transition of the interpolation path from concave to convex in Fig. 6, as pre-training duration increases, is a particularly interesting phenomenon. The authors briefly suggest this may be related to the decreasing Frobenius norm of the difference between the weights of the maths and petext checkpoints. Could the authors elaborate on this hypothesis in more detail?

One of the goals of the present work was to use the spectral information about weight matrices of pre-trained models as a theoretical foundation for explaining the domain connectivity phenomenon. We have established that changes in weight matrices during the CPT stage can be attributed to changing directions of singular vectors; furthermore, the singular vectors with the largest changes are associated with singular values near the peaks in singular spectra. However, we have discovered that the spectral structure of attention heads of large pre-trained models is more complex than the heavy-tailed self-regularization theory assumes, and the regions of singular value spectra corresponding to the changing vectors become more narrow as the pre-train token budget increases. We tentatively hypothesize that the presence of such increasingly narrow peaks in the singular spectra of heads makes associated singular vectors quasi-degenerate, enables domain connectivity and results in lower Frobenius norm of CPT deltas. However, further development of quantitative theory for domain connectivity requires more sophisticated models for the spectra of pre-trained models - we consider it an interesting research direction for further work.

summary.value:
This paper studies the spectrum changes of parameter matrices via SVD during Continual Pre-training (CPT), an important stage in modern LLM development. It has several interesting findings, e.g., CPT injects new knowledge primarily by rotating the singular vectors of the weight matrices, rather than altering their singular values; the identification of domain connectivity; head-wise sparsity.

The review evaluation of this paper is a bit mixed. Some reviewers complain about the limited experiments (e.g., a single model architecuture) and the authors have conducted additional experiments during the rebuttal. I have read this paper by myself and admit that this paper has some interesting findings but the analysis/thoughts are not significant, as mentioned by one reviewer "lack of theoretical depth". For example, when checking Figure 1, I suggest the authors to present the scaling laws of CPT, and compare them with standard pre-training. The findings can be more concentrated. I suggest the authors to follow the scaling laws paper to polish the findings, the paper structure as well as the title. The current title is quite unclear.

After my own reading, this paper falls into a borderline (with both pros and cons). There are some stuffs that should have been done during the submission. For example, the experiments are extended beyond just one single model size and architecture. The authors did this during the rebuttal. I finally decide to reject this paper but I strongly suggest the authors to carefully polish the paper to make it more sigificant and impactful in this community.

Thank you for taking the time to review the paper and provide feedback.
 
> The study is conducted on a single model size (1B) and a single architecture (OLMo 2). It is unclear whether the findings generalize to other model architectures

Per your suggestion, we have carried out the experiments with on 7B parameters models. It has allowed us to confirm our key findings. For details, and for our reasoning for choosing OLMo backbone, please refer to the general comment above, and to the updated sections 4.4 and 4.5 in main text. 

> The most effective head-pruning strategy presented is a "greedy" rewind based on single-head impact (Fig 7(a)). This method appears to be computationally prohibitive, as it seems to require a separate evaluation for every head.
              
We use the greedy rewind as ground truth for evaluating different scalar criteria for heads importance; we do not suggest it to be used as a practical recipe. All other methods, however, require only computation of one or several scalar metrics per head, and are much more computationally expedient and applicable to any reasonable model size. 
 
> Does the increasing convexity has anything to do with learning rate? Did you run different token budget in totally separate experiments, or using early checkpoints as model for smaller token budget?
 
For all of our pre-train experiments on 1B model: 20B, 100B, 400B, we run separate and complete scheduler cycles, in order for the results to be compatible with the 4T pre-train provided by the OLMo team.
 
We thank you again for your feedback and look forward to addressing any other questions or concerns you might have.

Thank you for your constructive feedback. We address the questions and concerns below.
 
> Q1: Statistical robustness  reproducibility. Report mean ± std (or bootstrap CIs) across multiple random seeds for all key curves/thresholds (e.g., head removal, SVD truncation, interpolation results). Add exact seeds and number of repeats in the appendix.

We have added extra experiments with different random seeds for head-level rewind, which we demonstrate on new Figure 5. For SVD truncation and interpolation, the procedures are defined by a pair of CPT checkpoints; the computational requirements for CPT are prohibitive for running multiple random seeds. To ensure reproducibility, we confirm qualitative finding across multiple domains: math, instruction+QA, code and model scales: 1B and 7B.

For metrics computation, we estimate performance variability using an 80\% bootstrap procedure with 5 seeds, applied to models after 20B-token Stage~2 continual pre-training on the DolminoMath dataset. Results for both the 1B and 7B models are summarized in table below. We observe that the variance in metrics computation is small to affect the conclusions drawn in the paper. 

| Model | GSM8K           | DROP              |
|-------|-------------------|------------------|
| 7B    | 0.698 ± 0.005     | 0.437 ± 0.015  |
| 1B    | 0.534 ± 0.009     | 0.232 ± 0.006  |

> Q2: Dataset / evaluation choices. If feasible, add other benchmarks (additional math datasets, code or reasoning tasks) to test generality.
 
> Q3: Architecture / scale generality. Demonstrate (or empirically argue) that the reported spectral phenomena and domain-connectivity scaling hold beyond OLMo-2 1B — e.g., a different backbone or model scale, or provide a clear justification why OLMo-2 is representative.

Per your suggestion, we have carried out the experiments on additional domains: instruction data and code, as well as on 7B parameters models. It has allowed us to confirm the findings regarding domain connectivity, and to uncover attention head heterogeneity with regard to CPT behavior. For details, and for our reasoning for choosing OLMo backbone please refer to the general comment above, and to the updated sections 4.4 and 4.5 in the main text.

> Q4: Mechanistic claims need stronger evidence. Provide a clearer mechanistic hypothesis or conduct targeted control experiments (shuffled/noise data, optimizer ablations, perturbation tests) before asserting causal explanations.

In this work we focus on the empirical study of CPT properties across several domains and model sizes, which allows us to establish novel phenomena of domain connectivity and head heterogeneity. We provide tentative hypotheses for these findings, based on the observation that the singular vectors with the largest changes are associated with singular values near the peaks in singular spectra, and these peaks become more narrow as the pre-train token budget increases. We refrain from asserting causal explanations, since providing the theoretical explanation of the observed properties would require further development of model spectra for pre-trained models, which we leave for further research.

> Q5: Practical guidance safety of sparsification. Expand discussion on how to choose heads/singular values safely (per-layer heterogeneity, CPT token budget dependence), and evaluate risks for downstream / rare tasks to avoid misapplication of pruning advice.

In this work we focus on properties of the CPT delta and its effect on the metrics which demonstrate marked change after domain CPT. We note that this set of metrics is different from those typically assessed after a full cycle of model training which includes SFT and RL stages. Before addressing the downstream effects, which is a separate substantial body of research, we plan to investigate more pressing questions related to the applicability of task arithmetic framework for CPT, and to the origins of difference in quality between CPT model soups and CPT on mixture of data from several domains.

We thank the reviewers for taking their valuable time to provide constructive feedback on the paper. We sincerely apologize for delaying the responses compared to the provided guidelines due to technical issues with the computational hardware. We have expanded the experiments to include other domains and models scales - it has allowed us to confirm our findings and to uncover novel phenomena.
 
In order to address the comments regarding the generalizability of the results, we have conducted additional experiments - we extend the set of domains of CPT to include:
a) instruction following and question answering, for which we carry out CPT on a mixture of FLAN and StackExchangeQA datasets. Following the OLMo paper, we refer to this CPT as "Instruct";
b) code - for which we carry out CPT on a subset of StarCoder dataset. 
Additionally, we carry out experiments on a 7B model with OLMo backbone on the same domains. Full details are provided in Section 3 of the main text. We confirm our hypotheses of domain connectivity and head specialization for multiple domains and model scales.
 
Expanding the scope of the study according to the suggestions provided by the reviewers has allowed us to uncover additional novel findings - more specifically, to establish the existence of heterogeneity in the behavior of attention heads along the CPT trajectory, which is amplified with increasing pre-train budget.  We can roughly divide the attention heads into three groups: those with small to no changes, those with substantial changes for any CPT domain, and those exhibiting different amount of change depending on the domain. Moreover, we have developed criteria for ranking attention heads according to their influence on domain CPT quality by comparing the degree of change of heads after CPT on the target domain and reference text CPT. In order to accomodate new findings we carried out reorganization of text for better readability by changing places of chapters 4.4 and 4.5 and updating figures across the manuscript.

Regarding the experiments with other stacks - for our study we needed open-source models with available checkpoints before the CPT stage of the pre-train pipeline - otherwise, we would need to re-run entire pipeline up to CPT, which imposes prohibitive resource requirements. This factor limited our choice to Pythia, SmolLM, Amber, MAP Neo. Among these models, OLMo demonstrates very high quality, almost on par with LLaMA and Qwen. Moreover, model size and pre-train data are more substantial drivers of quality compared to technical differences in architecture. That's why we have prioritized allocation of our computational resources to experiments with novel domains and 7B OLMo model.
 
We would be happy to address any other questions or concerns the reviewers might have and to provide further clarifications.

comment.value:
Dear ICLR Conference Chairs,

In appreciation of your valuable time, and due to a change in the rebuttal logistics resulting in an increase of your workload, we would like to provide you with a concise summary of our work, reviewers' concerns, and the results of addressing them.

In the first preprint draft we report the results of investigating the continual pre-training (CPT) stage for the 1B-parameter OLMo model on math and text domains. We have: 1) identified a novel phenomenon of **domain connectivity** -- the ability to interpolate between checkpoints after CPT on different domains without quality loss, 2) observed that CPT works by updating singular vectors, 3) demonstrated that the parameter updates can be significantly sparsified. 

In response to reviewer feedback regarding the generalizability of our results, we have extended experiments to 7B models and new CPT domains: instruction and code. We have **confirmed our findings**, and have discovered the phenomenon of **head heterogeneity** in the behavior of attention matrices during CPT on different domains. Further, we propose a method for estimating the influence of attention heads, which results in up to **4% quality increase** or 60% head sparsification for math CPT of a 7B model. 

We address all other reviewer questions as well, please see below for more details; we would be happy to address any additional questions or comments. We hope that our work and open-sourced analysis framework can serve as a foundation for further research into improving the LLM training methodology.

Thank you!

> W3: Practical Implications of Sparsity: While the paper's main contribution is clearly its scientific insight into how continual pre-training works, it would be even stronger if it also discussed how these findings could be applied in practice, especially the "high rank yet compressible" characteristic of the CPT delta. Such a discussion would make the work more useful to a wider audience.
 
> Q3: On the redundancy and compressibility of the CPT delta: The paper finds the CPT delta to be high rank, yet simultaneously compressible. This appears to contrast with the fundamental assumptions of low rank adaptation methods like LoRA, which are mainly used in supervised fine tuning (SFT). Could the authors discuss the similarities and differences between this "high rank yet compressible" characteristic of the CPT delta and the common observation that SFT delta are typically low rank? Furthermore, could insights from this comparison be leveraged to develop more efficient CPT strategies?
 
We would like to highlight the difference in the typical token budget for SFT and CPT: for the former, the typical experiment runs for  hundreds of millions of tokens, while for CPT the typical token budget is in the tens of billions of tokens. This difference was the motivation for us to investigate the CPT properties in the first place, since CPT spectral properties are relatively less studied. Given the vast token budget of CPT, we hypothesized that it might be inherently less amenable to LoRA methods designed for the different regime of SFT; this is further supported by our experiments on SVD truncation. These considerations informed our decision to deprioritize LoRA experiments for CPT in this work.

From a practical standpoint, the feasibility of combining different continual pre-training (CPT) checkpoints analogously to task aritmetic method is an important question, which motivates our study of domain connectivity. We empirically observe that a simple CPT model soup performs worse than a dedicated CPT on a mixed domain - reasons for this are most likely tied to the complex spectral structure of pre-train models and is an interesting topic for further research.

summary.value: The paper investigates how continual pre-training (CPT) infuses domain knowledge into large language models through spectral analysis of attention heads. Using OLMo-2-1B as a testbed, the authors find that domain adaptation primarily rotates singular vectors rather than changing singular values, and that many heads or singular components can be pruned with minimal loss. The analysis is supported by the open-source toolkit NetInspect.

strengths.value:
- **Relevant topic:** Understanding how domain-specific knowledge is absorbed in LLMs is timely and valuable.
- **Systematic analysis:** Provides multiple spectral diagnostics (norms, ranks, SVD fits, vector agreement).
- **Open-source toolkit:** The release of *NetInspect* adds reproducibility and utility for future research.
- **Empirical findings:** Observations on head-level redundancy and domain connectivity are potentially insightful for model merging and interpretability.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Statistical robustness & reproducibility.** Report mean ± std (or bootstrap CIs) across multiple random seeds for all key curves/thresholds (e.g., head removal, SVD truncation, interpolation results). Add exact seeds and number of repeats in the appendix.
2. **Dataset / evaluation choices.** If feasible, add other benchmarks (additional math datasets, code or reasoning tasks) to test generality.
3. **Architecture / scale generality.** Demonstrate (or empirically argue) that the reported spectral phenomena and domain-connectivity scaling hold beyond OLMo-2 1B — e.g., a different backbone or model scale, or provide a clear justification why OLMo-2 is representative.
4. **Mechanistic claims need stronger evidence.**  Provide a clearer mechanistic hypothesis or conduct targeted control experiments (shuffled/noise data, optimizer ablations, perturbation tests) before asserting causal explanations. 
5. **Practical guidance & safety of sparsification.** Expand discussion on how to choose heads/singular values safely (per-layer heterogeneity, CPT token budget dependence), and evaluate risks for downstream / rare tasks to avoid misapplication of pruning advice.

summary.value: This paper investigates the key phenomena occurring during Continual Pre-training (CPT), an important stage in modern LLM development. The authors observe that the pre-training stage alters the internal structure of the model's weight matrices, forming a complex singular value spectrum in the attention heads that simple random matrix theories cannot adequately describe. Furthermore, the paper posits that CPT injects new knowledge primarily by rotating the singular vectors of the weight matrices, rather than altering their singular values. Key findings include the identification of domain connectivity, which is the ability to interpolate between checkpoints after CPT on different domains, and the discovery of head-wise sparsity in the model increment that encodes new domain knowledge. The paper also provides an open source implementation to ensure reproducibility.

strengths.value:
1. Significance: The CPT stage has received far less attention than supervised fine-tuning (SFT). This study offers valuable new insights into the mechanisms of domain adaptation that occur during CPT.  
2. Quality and Clarity: The experimental design is rigorous and thorough. The figures are clear and informative.  
3. Reproducibility: The appendix provides extensive details supporting reproducibility, and the authors offer an open-source implementation to ensure that the results can be reliably reproduced.

summary.value: This paper analyzes how LLMs learn domain knowledge during Continual Pre-Training (CPT) using spectral analysis (SVD) on the weight deltas of 1B models. The authors identify two key findings: (1) "domain connectivity," showing that models CPT-trained on different domains (e.g., math and text) can be linearly interpolated, and this interpolation quality improves significantly with longer base model pre-training. (2) Head-wise sparsity, demonstrating that a significant fraction (up to 35%) of attention heads in the CPT delta are redundant and can be rewound to their pre-trained values without significant performance loss. The paper also provides the important insight that domain adaptation occurs primarily via singular vector rotation, while the singular value spectrum remains stable.

strengths.value:
1. Novelty and Significance of "Domain Connectivity": The paper's contribution is identifying "domain connectivity" in CPT models and showing that the quality of this linear interpolation becomes more convex (i.e., better) with longer pre-training. This is a key insight for the entire lifecycle of LLM development.

2. The paper provides concrete, quantitative results on the redundancy of CPT deltas. Finding that 35% of heads can be rewound and 20% of the delta's singular values can be truncated is impactful for future work on efficient adaptation and merging.

3. The paper provides code for both the experiments and the NetInspect analysis library.

weaknesses.value:
1. The study is conducted on a single model size (1B) and a single architecture (OLMo 2). It is unclear whether the findings generalize to other model architecture
2. The most effective head-pruning strategy presented is a "greedy" rewind based on single-head impact (Fig 7a). This method appears to be computationally prohibitive, as it seems to require a separate evaluation for every head.
